Key Points and More
  • State-driven programs could be controlled by if/else blocks, switches, or by state objects that implement a common interface.
  • If/else blocks and switch blocks are easier to write for small programs with fewer states. But in a program with a large number of states, controlling how and when to switch between states is harder using if/else blocks or switch blocks. Also, because the state must be checked every time through the game loop, a large number of states may slow down the game.
  • State objects that implement a common State interface might be more efficient because the game loop never has to test the game's state. The game automatically calls the correct code for the state, by calling one of the required methods in the State interface.
  • It is also easy to add additional states to a program that uses state objects, without affecting code already written for the other states. Often if you need to add states to a program controlled by a switch block, corresponding changes must also be made to the code that handles other states.
  • State objects allow more features than a switch block because each state can implement several possible actions. This project had methods for entering the state, performing a repeatable action in the state, and exiting the state. Depending on the kind of object for which you are providing the states, you might require different methods or different numbers of methods than the states used to implement this game. For example, the game itself might have game states that implement methods named run(), and updateData().
  • To use state objects for state-driven programming, first create an interface to define the state, naming all of its required methods. For example, to create an interface named GameState with methods named run() and updateData():
public interface GameState {
  public void run();
  public void updateData();
}
  • Next, implement that interface in classes, one for each possible state. Each state must then provide code for all the methods in the interface. For example, a game may have a load state, a play game state, and an end game state. To create a state named LoadState:
public class LoadState implements GameState {
  public void run () {
    ...
  }
  public void updateData () {
    ...
  }
}
  • Next, your program should create instance variables for each state and an instance variable to hold the current state. For example, if possible state classes are named LoadState, PlayGameState, and EndGameState, and they all implement the interface named GameState, and you want to store the current state, loadState, in an instance variable named currentState:
public LoadState loadState = new LoadState();
public PlayGameState playGameState = new PlayGameState();
public EndGameState endGameState = new EndGameState();
public GameState currentState = loadState
  • Next, your game loop should call one or more of the methods on the variable that holds the current state. For example, calling the run() method on the above defined currentState will result in calling the run() method of loadState(), playGameState(), or endGameState(), depending on which object was most recently assigned to currentState:
currentState.run();
  • Finally, the code that runs for each state should change the state when necessary. For example, if the game should end when pieces is 0:
if (pieces == 0) {
  currentState = endGameState;
}
  • The Cat and Mouse program added a step to the above process. Changing state needed to always first run the code to exit the previous state, then set the state to the new state, then run the code to enter the new state. If setting the state should perform a sequence of steps, provide a method to set the state. For example, if changing the GameState should always call updateData() from the old state before switching to a new state, use
private void setState(GameState newGameState) {
  currentState.updateData();
  currentState = newGameState();
}

Project 8 - Blitz
In this project, you'll learn to separate program logic from user interface implementation, using a model/view/controller design.
The model contains the logic of the game, but no user interface. The model defines objects, including a deck of cards and multiple players, but cannot draw those objects. The model also controls the flow of the game using state-driven design, based on the rules for playing Blitz.
The view is a JFrame with panels and buttons. Without game logic, the view displays just text, images, and shapes, and can move them around on the screen. The view also recognizes mouse clicks, which is how the user enters his choices.
The model and view communicate with each other through the controller. The controller must convert the card objects into images, tell the view what must be moved on the screen based on instructions from the model, and tell the model what action to take based on choices made by the user in the view.
Blitz, also known as Scat or 31, is a card game with a goal to get 31 points in one suit, or rap, a signal that you think someone else has a worse hand than you. Players lose one of their three tokens every time they lose to a blitz or rap. But beware, if the player who raps also has the worst hand, he must pay double.

Try It - Make Room for the Players
The two computer player areas should be placed at the top of the window, the human player area at the bottom, and the deck and discard pile in the middle. Each player's area should show the player's name, up to 4 cards below his name, up to 3 tokens below the cards, and additional text information below the tokens. A 4-pixel space should be displayed between cards, a gap of 20 pixels should be displayed between players, and a margin of 10 pixels should be shown around the edges of the window. The text will have a font size of 20, and cards will be the height of the images in the BlitzController class. The spacing and font size will be used by another class, so should be public.
  1. Create in the blitz.view package a new class named GamePanel, which uses JPanel as its superclass and has no stub code.
    1. Use Quick Fix to add a private static final long integer variable named serialVersionUID, set to 1L.
    2. Add a public static final integer variable named SPACING, set to 4.
    3. Add a private static final integer variable named GAP, set to 20.
    4. Add a private static final integer variable named MARGIN, set to 10.
    5. Add a public static final integer variable named FONT_SIZE, set to 20.
    6. Add a private static final integer variable named CARD_WIDTH, set to the width of a card in BlitzController. (Hint: use BlitzController's CARD_WIDTH variable.)
    7. Add a private static final integer variable named CARD_HEIGHT, set to the height of a card in BlitzController. (Hint: use BlitzController's CARD_HEIGHT variable.)
    8. Add a private static final integer variable named PLAYER_WIDTH, set to the width of 4 cards plus the spacings between them. (Hint: use CARD_WIDTH and SPACING.)
    9. Add a private static final integer variable named PLAYER_HEIGHT, set to a card height, 3 rows of text, plus the spacings between them. (Hint: use CARD_HEIGHT, FONT_SIZE, and SPACING.)
    10. Add a private static final integer variable named WIDTH, set to 2 player widths, a gap between them, plus a margin on each side of the window. (Hint: use PLAYER_WIDTH, GAP, and MARGIN.)
    11. Add a private static final integer variable named HEIGHT, set to the total of: 2 player heights, a card height, gaps above and below the middle card, and margins at the top and bottom of the window. (Hint: use PLAYER_HEIGHT, CARD_HEIGHT, GAP, and MARGIN.)

Try It - Add Players to the View
Each player's area needs room for the player's name, up to four cards, up to 3 tokens, and additional information to identify whether he got a blitz or rapped. The token area will draw either tokens or text. However, the y-value for drawing shapes is the upper left corner of the shape, but the y-value for drawing text is the base line of the text. So even though shapes and text will be displayed in the same area, different y-values must be provided for each.
  1. Create in the blitz.view package a new class named PlayerView, which uses no superclass and has no stub code.
    1. Add a private static final integer variable named CARD_WIDTH, set to the width of a card in BlitzController. (Hint: use BlitzController's CARD_WIDTH variable.)

    5. Add a private static final integer variable named TOKEN_SIZE, set to 10.
    6. Add a private static final integer variable named TOKEN_Y_OFFSET, set to the sum of the height of a card plus the spaces, one above and one below the card. (Hint: use CARD_HEIGHT, and SPACING.)

In the game of Blitz, a player may continue playing even when he has no tokens. However, if such a player is supposed to lose one or more tokens, theoretically resulting in a number of tokens less than zero, he would be out of the game. A player having no tokens is considered to be “Riding” and a player who would have a negative value for tokens is considered to be “Out”. Key Points and More
  • The view presents the game information to the user and is how the user provides input into the game.
  • The controller contains the main() method, tells the view what to add or update in the display, requests user input from the view, and responds to user input from the view.
  • The view for the Blitz game is a Java Swing view, using a JFrame and other components. The Swing components can display only text, images, and shapes, but can move them around on the screen as directed by the controller. The Swing components can also monitor for mouse clicks and other events.
  • The view should include no game logic, only details of how the window is laid out for the user to interact with the game.

    • Determine the card's speed and direction.

The loop you just created runs only once because the loop is defined to stop when the card is moving, and the code in the loop sets the card to not moving.
Next, check if the card has reached its x destination or y destination. If it has not yet reached either destination, the card should continue moving.
The card will have reached its x destination if the card is moving to the right and its current location is greater than the final x destination, or if it is moving to the left and its current location is less than the final x destination. In either case, set the card's current x location to the desired final x location. If the card has not yet reached its x destination, it should continue moving.
The card will have reached its y destination if the card is moving down and its current location is greater than the final y destination, or if it is moving up and its current location is less than the final y destination. In either case, set the card's current y location to the desired final y location. If the card has not yet reached its y destination, it should continue moving.
In moveCard(),
  1. Move the remaining two comments, about stopping movement, to the end of the while loop.
  2. After the comment to stop X movement if the X movement went too far:
    1. If incrementX is greater than 0 and cardX is greater than endX, or if incrementX is less than 0 and cardX is less than endX:
      1. Set cardX to endX.
    2. Otherwise:
      1. Set cardIsMoving to true.
  3. After the comment to stopY movement if the Y movement went too far:
    1. If incrementY is greater than 0 and cardY is greater than endY, or if incrementY is less than 0 and cardY is less than endY:
      1. Set cardY to endY.
    2. Otherwise:
      1. Set cardIsMoving to true.

Key Points and More
  • One way to slow down animation is by putting the thread to sleep between each iteration of the animation loop. Another way is to use a Timer. Both were demonstrated in earlier lessons in this book.
  • Why did I put the thread to sleep instead of use a Timer in this game? A timer uses a background thread, which allows the main thread to continue running while the timer thread runs. In contrast, this game must pause while a card is moved. Otherwise, the next card movement would start before the first card movement was completed.
  • Calling SwingUtilities' invokeLater() method from main() placed the main thread of this program on the EDT. As you learned earlier, doing so is advised for any program that uses Java Swing.
  • Calling Thread's sleep() method on the main thread puts the EDT to sleep, which is not advised for any program that uses Java Swing because doing so blocks the EDT. No other window updates can be made nor can any other events be responded to while the the EDT is sleeping. You may have noticed that if you try to close the window for Blitz, the window won't close until the program has finished dealing the cards.
    • As you saw in this lesson, putting the thread to sleep from the constructor interrupted painting the initial window.
      • One way to solve this is to wait until after the window is constructed and visible before the thread is put to sleep. This could be accomplished by starting the game from a button on the window, or in response to a message displayed from a JOptionPane.
      • Another way would be to start a new thread to call the method that puts the thread to sleep. Then the new thread instead of the EDT would be put to sleep.
  • Swing combines multiple repaint requests into one if they are submitted closely together. To ensure that one repaint is processed completely before a following repaint is processed, use paintImmediately() instead of repaint().
  • Animation may be slowed down by using one of several techniques:
    • Use a Timer. This prevents conflicts with the EDT. However, be aware that the timer runs on a different thread. The current thread will continue running while the code in the run() method of the timer is running.
    • Use Thread.sleep(). However, be aware that if code does this from the EDT, other repaint and event requests will be blocked until until the thread is done sleeping.
    • Use paintImmediately() instead of repaint(). This will force the paint request, but will still block the EDT from processing any previously submitted repaint and event requests.
    • Run in a different thread the code that calls the animation loop. However, be aware that the new thread will run concurrently with other threads. Be sure to put all the code that you want to run in sequence in a single thread. For example, to move a card from the deck to a player and then move another card from that same player to the discard, both steps could run in one thread, both calling the same move() method. However, if processing the next player is not on the same thread, the next player might take his turn before the first player's turn is done. Both players might then move a card at the same time.
    • Run in a different thread the code that calls the animation loop, and synchronize the method that has the animation loop. To synchronize a method, use the synchronized modifier in the method declaration. For example, to synchronize the move() method:
private synchronized void move(int beginX, int beginY, int endX, int endY) {
    • A synchronized method is locked when accessed so only one thread can access it at a time. However, if a method is called by more than two threads, the order the threads happen to access the method is not guaranteed.
      Synchronizing the loop to move the card could not be used for the Blitz project because players must not be allowed to play out of turn. The Blitz project uses one thread for players and one thread for the animation loop. If players 1, 2, and 3 sequentially try to move a card, player 1 will move a card. Because the animation loop is on a separate thread, player 2 will try to move next but can't because player 1 has a lock on moving the card. And now player 3 takes his turn. But if player 1 isn't done moving yet, and both player 2 and player 3 are waiting to move the card, there is no guarantee who gets to move the card first.
    • Place the entire process in a separate thread. For example, I could have placed all the code that runs in the BlitzModel on a separate thread, thus ensuring that everything ran in sequence and in the correct order. But then much more code would have been required to make sure all Swing components were created and handled on the EDT.
    • Threads can be managed with other techniques, but those techniques are beyond the scope of this book.

Key Points and More

Try It - Add States to the Model
Program states will be distinguished by integer values representing:
  • time to wait for input
  • start a new hand
  • deal cards
  • the computer's turn to draw
  • the computer's turn to discard
  • the next player's turn
  • my turn to draw
  • my turn to discard
  • settle a rap
  • settle a blitz
  • check whether the game is over
State values for my turn to draw and for my turn to discard must be public so the controller may access them.

Because this project uses a large number of states, an interface would be better than a switch block for managing the state. However, the intent of this project is to demonstrate how to separate the user interface from the game logic. Managing the state with an interface would involve creating many more classes and make this program much larger than what is needed to teach the intended lesson. Therefore, use the easier-to-write switch block to manage the game state.
Add a method that calls the appropriate method based on the state of the game.
  1. Add a public method named play(). It should take no parameters and return nothing.
    1. Set up a switch block to check the value of state.
      1. If the value is STATE_NEW_HAND:
        1. Call newHand(), passing no arguments.
      2. If the value is STATE_DEAL:
        1. Call deal(), passing no arguments.
      3. If the value is STATE_NEXT_PLAYER:
        1. Call nextPlayer(), passing no arguments.
      4. If the value is STATE_COMPUTER_DRAW:
        1. Call computerDraw(), passing no arguments.

The computer player should take the discard if the discard will improve the player's hand. How can you most easily determine whether picking up a card would improve a hand?
  • If the discard stack is not empty:
    • Check the points in the hand without the discard.
    • Add the discard to the hand.
    • Remove the lowest card in the hand.
    • Check the points in the hand again.
    • If the hand now has more points, the discard improved the hand.
    • Put the cards back as they were.
Go back to BlitzModel.

Try It - Settle a Rap
A player must rap before drawing a card. If a player raps, he does not get to draw a card, and play should move to the next player, continuing in clockwise order. After someone raps, each other player should get one more turn. When play gets back to the person who rapped, points are calculated for everyone's hand. The player with the fewest points loses 1 token. If no one has fewer points than the player who rapped, the player who rapped should lose 2 tokens and no one else lose any tokens, even if they have the same number of points as the player who rapped.
After the rap is settled, the next player to the left of the current dealer and still in the game should be the next dealer.
Go back to BlitzModel.
  1. Add a public method named getNextDealerId(). It should take no parameters and return an integer.
    1. Create a boolean named done, set to false.
    2. Create an integer named nextDealerId, set to the result of the sum dealerId plus 1, modulo numberOfPlayers.
    3. While done is false:
      1. If the players element at index nextDealerId is not out: (Hint: use Player's isOut() method.)
        1. Set done to true.
      2. Otherwise:
        1. Set nextDealerId to the result of the sum nextDealerId plus 1, modulo numberOfPlayers.
    4. Return nextDealerId.

Key Points and More
  • Model/view/controller design organizes code into 3 separate categories:
    • The model holds the game objects and controls the flow of action based on the rules of the game.
    • The view presents the game information to the user and allows user input into the game.
    • The controller provides interpretation of the data and the flow of information between the model and the view.
  • For every action the model takes that the program user should be aware of, the model must notify the controller. The controller must then notify the view of the action, after converting the data provided by the model into a form the view can use.
  • For every action the user takes with the view, the view must notify the controller. The controller must then notify the model, after converting the data provided by the view into a form the model can use.
  • In the Blitz game:
    • The model has a deck of cards and multiple players. The model also controls the flow of the game using state-driven design, based on the rules for playing Blitz.
    • The view is a Java JFrame that can display text, images, and shapes, and can move them around in the window. The view also recognize mouse clicks, which is how the user enters his choices.
    • The controller must convert the card objects into images, tell the view what must be presented and moved in the window based on instructions from the model, and tell the model what action to take based on choices made by the user.
  • Some programmers disagree whether the controller or the model should contain the game loop that controls the flow of the game. I chose to put the game loop in the model because I see the flow of the program as very much part of the logic and rules of the game. I wanted to contain all the logic of the game in the model, leaving the controller to only interpret and send information back and forth between the view and the model. This game might have been easier to write had I put game flow into the controller rather than in the model. But I think the model is easier to reuse if the game flow is in the model.
  • Some programmers disagree whether or not the objects should be used to pass data into the view. For example, this game would have been a lot easier to write if the controller had passed the Card and Player objects to the View instead of converting them to BufferedImages and integer IDs. But again, I think the controller and view might be easier to reuse for other games if the controller and view are not so specifically tied to the Blitz Card and Blitz Player.
  • You may choose to separate the model, view, and controller code differently for other programs.
  • Using a model/view/controller design makes it much easier to create additional versions of the game to run with different user interfaces.
    • This Blitz game runs using a Java Swing user interface so the game could be run on a computer that uses a Windows, MAC OSX, or Linux operating system.
    • You could use the same model with a different view and controller to create a text version or 3-D version of the game.
    • Or you could use the same model with a different view and controller to create the game as an app for an Android device.
    • Or maybe some day you could use the same model with a different view and controller to play the game against a robot.
    • In all cases, the logic of the game would remain the same and is already neatly bundled in the model.
  • Using the model/view/controller design makes it easier to divide a larger project across a team. The user interface and game logic could easily be written by different people.
  • Using the model/view/controller design makes it easier to adapt the view for other projects. The BlitzView could easily be adapted for more players, for games that need areas to lay down cards, use decks of cards with different point values, and more.
  • Using the model/view/controller design results in a much larger program. The Blitz game could have been much easier to write, using a lot less code, if each object combined its own logic and view, much like the previous programs in this book. But then the program wouldn't have had any of the advantages listed above.
Lesson 8.5 - Reuse Game Logic
Since you've completely separated the Blitz game logic from the user interface, the logic could be used with any other user interface. Each new user interface (view) would require a new controller to handle communications between the model and the view. In this lesson you'll prepare the Blitz model to be used with a different controller.

Key Points and More
  • Use an Interface to define required methods.
  • In the Blitz game, the BlitzController interface was defined with all the methods that the BlitzModel called on the controller.
  • The BlitzModel may then refer to the BlitzController interface instead of the BlitzControllerSwing class. In that way, the model will work with any controller class that implements the BlitzController interface.
  • To create another controller for a different view for the Blitz game, the controller must implement the BlitzController interface. To interact with the Blitz model, the controller must at some point call the following methods in BlitzModel:
    • start() - to start the game. This method has no parameters.
    • myPlayerDrewCard() - when the user performed an action on the view to draw a card. This method has no parameters.
    • myPlayerTookDiscard() - when the user performed an action on the view to take the discard. This method has no parameters.
    • myPlayerDiscarded() - when the user performed an action on the view to discard a card. This method has one parameter—the index of the card the user wants to discard.

I Hope You Enjoyed this Book
I enjoy programming. As you've probably guessed, based on the kinds of programs I've put into my Do-It-Yourself Java Games books, I enjoy doing puzzles and playing games. To me, writing a computer game is like solving a puzzle. But as I work my way through these “puzzles,” I get to (have to) play the games I enjoy, giving me double the puzzle/game entertainment. Plus, I get to make the games work the way I want them to work. Therefore, for all these reasons, computer game programming is the ultimate puzzle for me. I hope writing these games has inspired you to try writing your own games, too.
If you enjoyed this book:
  • Lend it - This book is set up to allow lending. Please share it with a friend.
  • Recommend it - Help others find this book by recommending it to friends, readers’ groups, and discussion boards.
  • Review it - Tell others why you liked this book. Review it on Amazon. If you do write a review, please send me a copy in an email to diyjava@godtlandsoftware.com, so I can personally thank you.
If you liked this book, you might be interested in the next book I have planned for this series: Do-It-Yourself Multi-Player Java Games: An Introduction to Java Sockets and Internet-Based Games. This fourth book in the Do-It-Yourself Java Games series will use the same fill-in-the-blank approach to teach Java computer programming. You will use many of the skills taught in the first three books to create games that can be played between players on different computers, using the internet.
Good luck, and happy programming!
Annette Godtland

Other Books I've Written
Do-It-Yourself Java Games Series
In the Do-It-Yourself Java Games series of books, I use a "discovery learning" approach to teach computer programming: learn Java programming techniques more by doing Java programming than by reading about them. Through extensive use of fill-in blanks, with easy one-click access to answers, I guide you to write complete programs yourself, starting with the first lesson. You'll discover how, when, and why Java programs are written the way they are.
Do-It-Yourself Java Games: An Introduction to Java Computer Programming
“Do-It-Yourself Java Games: An Introduction to Java Computer Programming” is the first book in my “Do-It-Yourself Java Games” series. In this first book, I teach the basics of Java programming, as you create text-based puzzle and game programs, like: Choose An Adventure, Secret Code, Hangman, Crazy Eights, and many more. “Do-It-Yourself Java Games: An Introduction to Java Computer Programming” is available at amazon.com.
More Do-It-Yourself Java Games: An Introduction to Java Graphics and Event-Driven Programming
“More Do-It-Yourself Java Games: An Introduction to Java Graphics and Event-Driven Programming” is the second book in my Do-It-Yourself Java Games series. In event-driven programming, the program lays out all the game pieces, then waits. The user then takes an action and the program responds to that action, whatever that action may be, and in whatever order the actions are taken.
In this second book, you will create more colorful and interactive games as you learn to create windows and dialogs, to add buttons and input fields, to use images and drawings, and to respond to input such as key strokes and mouse clicks and drags. You’ll create 10 more games, including several tile puzzles, a maze, a dice game, a word game, a card game, and an image resizer program. “More Do-It-Yourself Java Games: An Introduction to Java Graphics and Event-Driven Programming” is available at amazon.com.
This Little Program Went to Market
I also wrote “This Little Program Went to Market: Create, Deploy, Distribute, Sell, and Market Software and More on the Internet at Little or No Cost to You”. This book provides a detailed tutorial of the tips, tools, and techniques I learned, for getting a program to market and for selling almost anything on the Internet. “This Little Program Went to Market: Create, Deploy, Distribute, Sell, and Market Software and More on the Internet at Little or No Cost to You” is available at amazon.com, Barnes and Noble, and many other book retailers.

Appendix A - Glossary
This glossary defines Java programming terms used in this book and lists the lessons that covered these topics. In some cases, lessons specifically designed to teach these topics are found in the other Do-It-Yourself Java Games books.
abstract class
An abstract class is a class that is intended for use only as a superclass. Objects cannot be created from abstract classes.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.2 - Create an Abstract Class.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.1 - Use State-Driven Programming, Detect Collisions of Non-Rectangular Shapes.
abstract method
An abstract method is a method with the abstract modifier and no code. Abstract methods must be declared within either an abstract class or an interface. Classes that extend an abstract class must provide code for all the abstract class's abstract methods.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.2 - Create an Abstract Class.
action listener
Action listeners are classes that extend the ActionListener class. They wait for ActionEvents.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.7 - Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
ActionEvent
An ActionEvent is an event caused by the program user clicking a button, a radio button, a check box, or a menu item, or by the user selecting an item from a list or pressing enter in a text field. Add an ActionListener to a component to run code when an ActionEvent occurs.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.7 - Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.3 - Event Source in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
ActionListener
An ActionListener waits for an ActionEvent from its assigned component. When an ActionEvent occurs, Java calls the ActionListener's actionPerformed() method.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.7 - Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
alpha
Colors can be created from four integer values: red, green, blue, and alpha. The alpha value, also known as the alpha channel, sets the transparency of a color. The alpha value can range from 0 through 255, where 0 is totally transparent and 255 is totally opaque.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.1 - Transparent Colors, PNG Images in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
animate
Animation may be performed by the user dragging an object on the screen with the mouse or by a thread moving or changing the appearance of an object.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.1 - Drag Objects, Use a Dictionary.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.3 - Reduce Animation Flicker.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.2 - Stop All Activity with a Sleeping Thread.
argument
An argument is the value passed into a method that has defined parameters, when the method is called. The method may then use that value in its code.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - Methods with Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.3 - Methods with Multiple Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
ArithmeticException
An ArithmeticException is an exception thrown when a program attempts to do arithmetic that is not allowed, such as divide by zero.
See Lesson 8.5 - Integer Subtraction, Multiplication, and Division in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
array
An array is one kind of Java list. Elements of an array may be either Java primitives or Java Objects, but they must all have the same type. The size of the array is set as part of the array declaration and cannot be changed.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.4 - Arrays in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 14.5 - Empty Array in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.1 - Use a Multi-Dimensional Array.
ArrayList
An ArrayList is one kind of Java list. An ArrayList can only hold Java Objects, not Java primitives, and all elements in the list must have the same type. The size of the ArrayList can be changed at any time by adding or removing elements.
See Lesson 15.5 - Array Lists in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
audio file
An audio file is a sound recording. To play a sound in Java, the audio file must be of type .wav or .au.
See Lesson 1.7 - Add Sound.
AudioInputStream
An AudioInputStream is an InputStream formatted for audio input. Its data can be played back in real time, or put into a Clip to be played back later.
See Lesson 1.7 - Add Sound.
background color
A component is filled with its background color before its text or other details are added in the foreground color.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.2 - Panels, Predefined Colors in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
block of code
A block of code is a group of zero or more lines of code, surrounded by curly brackets, { }.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
boolean
Boolean is a basic data type. A boolean variable can have only two possible values, true or false. To specify a boolean value in a program, type “true” or “false”, but without the quotation marks.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.5 - Boolean Data Type in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
BorderLayout
The BorderLayout is a layout best used whenever components should be arranged in these five areas: across the top (PAGE_START), across the bottom (PAGE_END), along the left side between the top and bottom (LINE_START), along the right side between the top and bottom (LINE_END), and in the center (CENTER). Only one component is allowed in each of these areas. A component will be stretched to fill its assigned area.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.1 - Border Layout in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
BoxLayout
The BoxLayout is a layout best used whenever any number of components should be arranged in a row (X_AXIS) or in a column (Y_AXIS). When Java lays out components in a BoxLayout, components in a row layout might get stretched vertically and the components in a column layout might get stretched horizontally.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.2 - Box Layout, Combined Layouts in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
break
A break statement may be used to break out of a switch statement or a loop instead of running the next line of code.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.2 - Switch Statements in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
BufferedImage
A BufferedImage is a Java object that allows access to image data. For example, individual pixels in the image may be changed.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.2 - Read Image Files, Subimages, Image Icons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - New Graphics, Scale an Image in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.1 - Transparent Colors, PNG Images in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
BufferedReader
A BufferedReader reads character data files more efficiently than FileReaders or InputStreamReaders. Therefore, FileReaders and InputStreamReaders are typically used to create BufferedReaders, and then programs read file data using BufferedReaders.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.2 - Read from a File, Catch Multiple Exceptions in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.7 - Put Data Files in the JAR File in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
BufferedWriter
A BufferedWriter writes to character data files more efficiently than FileWriters. Therefore, FileWriters are typically used to create BufferedWriters, and then programs write file data using the BufferedWriter.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.1 - Write to a File in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
build path
The build path is a list of all the other Java projects and code-containing libraries that the current Java project needs to use.
See Lesson 8.7 - Extend the DIYWindow Class in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Add a Project to the Build Path in Appendix D - Using Eclipse.
button
A button usually refers to a clickable component in a window. When the component is clicked, an ActionEvent is sent. If the program is listening for the event, the program will usually respond in some way. Use the JButton class to create a button or a JRadioButton to create a radio button.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.7 - Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.1 - A Custom Button, this in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.2 - In Focus Mark in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.1 - Buttons with Images in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.3 - Button Focus in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.6 - A Default Button in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
A button may also refer to one of the buttons on the mouse. For example, the left mouse button would be used for a left-click.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.3 - Move Objects in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
button group
A button group is used to create a set of radio buttons. Only one radio button in the group may be selected at a time. When a radio button in the group is selected, the previously selected radio button will be deselected. Use the ButtonGroup class to create a button group.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
ButtonGroup
ButtonGroup is the class used to define a button group.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
byte
Byte is a basic data type. A byte variable can hold integers values between -128 and 127. To specify a byte value in a program, type the value without the quotation marks.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Integer Data Type and Addition in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
call
When a method is called, the program runs the code defined by that method before running the code that follows the method call.
See Lesson 6.3 - Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
case
A case label marks the start of the code to be run when a switch statement expression evaluates to a value that matches the case value.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.2 - Switch Statements in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.4 - Switch Default in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.6 - Case without Break in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 15.1 - Switch Statement with Integers in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
cast
Cast converts an object of one type to another type. A cast operation is indicated by putting a new type in parentheses before the name of a variable defined with a different type. The variable's class must be a superclass of the type to which the object is being cast. If an object can't be cast to the new type, a run time error will occur.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.3 - Event Source in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
char
A char is a Java character variable.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 15.2 - Character Data Type in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
character
Character is a basic data type, declared in Java with “char”. A character variable can hold only a single character value. To specify a character value in a program, type the character surrounded with single quotation marks.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 15.2 - Character Data Type in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
class
A class is a blueprint from which objects are created. A class defines the information the object can hold and the actions the object can take.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.7 - Extend the DIYWindow Class in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Create a First Program in Appendix D - Using Eclipse.
class variable
A class variable has one copy of the variable shared by all instances of its declaring class. In contrast, each instance of a class has its own copy of an instance variable. A class variable may be used by any of the methods defined by that class, without the variable being passed to the methods as an argument. Both class variables and instance variables must be declared in the class definition, not within class methods. Class variables must be declared with the static modifier.
clickable
This book refers to an object as clickable if clicking the mouse on the displayed representation of the object will result in the program taking an action.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.1 - A Custom Button, this in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games
Clip
A clip is pre-loaded audio data, opened to an AudioInputStream, that can be played back at a desired time.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.7 - Add Sound.
See Lesson 6.1 - Use State-Driven Programming, Detect Collisions of Non-Rectangular Shapes.
See Lesson 7.4 - Use an Interface for State-Driven Design.
code
Code is a series of computer instructions that when run in sequence perform a desired task.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
collision detection
Collision detection is the process of checking for intersection between two objects on the screen.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.2 - Detect Collisions of Rectangular Shapes.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.1 - Use State-Driven Programming, Detect Collisions of Non-Rectangular Shapes.
color
Colors are made up of a combination of red, green, and blue hues, and sometimes an alpha value. The hue and alpha values each range from 0 through 255. The higher the hue number, the more of that hue is in the color. Java provides predefined color variables for commonly used colors.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.2 - Panels, Predefined Colors in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.6 - Custom Colors in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.1 - Transparent Colors, PNG Images in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
comment
Comments are notes put in code to explain what the code is intended to do, or to label sections of code. Comments are ignored when the program is run. Comments are denoted by lines that begin with // or groups of lines that begin with /* and end with */.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Comments in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
comment out
You can “comment out” lines of code by turning those lines into a comment. When you turn code into a comment, that code will be ignored since programs ignore comments(comment).
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Comments in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
component
A component is any window object that can be added to a Java window.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Add Text, Window Size in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.2 - Panels, Predefined Colors in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.7 - Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 3.1 - Text Areas in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 3.2 - Scroll Bars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.3 - Add and Remove Components in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.3 - Space Between Components in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.1 - Create a Standard Project and Class.
component listener
Component listeners are classes that extend the ComponentListener class. They wait for ComponentEvents.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
ComponentAdapter
A ComponentAdapter is a class that eases ComponentListener object creation. Using a ComponentAdapter, a programmer writes code only for the ComponentListener's methods that will be used, rather than having to write code for all the methods defined in ComponentListener. A ComponentAdapter may be used wherever a ComponentListener is required.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
ComponentEvent
A ComponentEvent is an event caused by a component changing size, location, or visibility. Add a ComponentListener or ComponentAdapter to a component to run code when the ComponentEvent occurs.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
ComponentListener
A ComponentListener waits for a ComponentEvent from its assigned component. When a ComponentEvent occurs, Java calls the ComponentListener's componentHidden(), componentMoved(), componentResized(), or componentShown() methods.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
confirm dialog
A confirm dialog is a dialog that asks the user a question and waits for an answer. Though a confirm dialog can request other combinations of answers, this book uses confirm dialogs that expect only a yes or no answer. Use JOptionPane to easily create a confirm dialog.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.4 - Confirm Dialogs in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
console
The console displays Java error messages, or the program's System.out messages. In Eclipse, the console is usually displayed in the bottom pane of the window.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - Try/Catch Blocks and Exceptions in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Print to the Console in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
constructor
A constructor is a special method that is called to create an object of that class.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 16.2 - Constructors in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
container
A container is a window component that can hold more than one component, including other containers. JFrame and JPanel are both container components.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Add Text, Window Size in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.3 - Multiple Panels, Preferred Size, Dimension in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
controller
In a model/view/controller design approach, the controller provides communication between the model and the view. The controller contains the main() method of the program, instructs the view about what to add or update in the display according to actions in the model, and sends user input from the view to the model.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Lay out the Display in the “View”.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - Set up Game Logic in the “Model”.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.5 - Reuse Game Logic.
coordinates
The coordinates of a Java object refer to its location in a container, specified by a pair of x and y values. A location may identify the placement of a window on the screen, or the placement of a component within another component. The x value is the number of pixels to the left edge of the object from the left edge of its container, and the y value is the number of pixels to the top of the object from the top edge of its container.
See Lesson 6.2 - Read Image Files, Subimages, Image Icons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - A Painted Panel: Color, Rectangles, Lines, Circles, and Preferred Size in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - New Graphics, Scale an Image in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.2 - Draw Strings, Font Metric in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
cursor
The mouse cursor is the symbol used to represent the location of the mouse pointer on the screen. You can change the mouse cursor to any image.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 3.1 - Change the Mouse Icon Dynamically.
Date
The Date class in Java represents a specific instant in time, exact to the nearest millisecond. When a new Date object is created with no parameter values, the Date object's time is set to the time maintained by the computer.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.4 - Current Date, Date Format in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
DateFormat
The Java DateFormat class represents many different kinds of date formats. DateFormat has methods that are common to all date formats. However, to work with a date format object, the program must first identify the type of the date format. A SimpleDateFormat is one kind of DateFormat.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.4 - Current Date, Date Format in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
declare
When you declare a variable, you state that the variable exists, assign the variable's properties, and optionally assign to the variable an initial value. The declaration of a method refers to the statement at the beginning of the method definition that lists the method's properties, return type, name, and parameters.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.3 - Variables, Strings, and the Escape Character in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.3 - Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - Methods with Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.3 - Methods that Return a Value in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Static Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.3 - Methods with Multiple Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
default button
The default button means the same as the default enter button.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.6 - A Default Button in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
default enter button
The default enter button is the button that will act as though it was clicked when someone presses the enter key, even when another component in the window has focus. For example, a window with input fields and a default enter button allows the program user to type in an input field and press the enter key to activate the default button without using the mouse.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.6 - A Default Button in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
define
When you define a class or method, you assign the class or method its properties, and provide code to implement the desired actions for the class or method.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.3 - Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - Methods with Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.3 - Methods that Return a Value in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.7 - Extend the DIYWindow Class in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Static Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.3 - Methods with Multiple Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
dialog
A dialog is a small window that displays a message or gets input from the user.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.8 - Message Dialogs in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.4 - Confirm Dialogs in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.2 - File Choosers in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.1 - A Custom Dialog in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.3 - Get Dialog Data in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
Dimension
A Dimension is a class that holds two integers, usually representing width and height.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.3 - Multiple Panels, Preferred Size, Dimension in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
disable
If a component is disabled, it will no longer listen for events or allow input.
See Lesson 9.2 - Box Layout, Combined Layouts in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
double
Double is a basic data type. A double variable can hold decimal numbers with as many as 16 decimal places. To specify a double value in a program, type the number including a decimal point but no quotation marks.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.6 - Double Data Type in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
double buffer
Animation is smoother if drawings are double buffered: first draw on an off-screen image, then paint the image to the screen. JPanels automatically double buffer by default.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.3 - Reduce Animation Flicker.
EDT
EDT is the abbreviation for the event dispatch thread.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.1 - Create a Standard Project and Class.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.5 - Create a Thread.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.6 - Stop a Thread.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 3.2 - Pause the Event Dispatch Thread.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.2 - Stop All Activity with a Sleeping Thread.
element
An element is a data item in an array or ArrayList. Refer to a specific element in an array or ArrayList by giving its index, its position in the array or ArrayList.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.4 - Arrays in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 14.5 - Empty Array in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Lesson 15.6 - Array Lists in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
ellipsis
An ellipsis is a series of three dots, …, usually used to indicate that some information has been omitted.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.3 - Font in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
Ellipses are used in the code listings in this book to represent lines of code that are not shown.
else block
An else block is an optional block of code added to the end of an if statement. The else block runs only if the if statement test evaluates to false.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.1 - If Statements, Strings that are Equal or Contain Letters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
enable
If a component is enabled, it will listen for events and allow input.
See Lesson 9.2 - Box Layout, Combined Layouts in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
escape character
The escape character (backslash, \,) is used to mark special characters in a string.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.4 - Joining Strings, the Escape Character in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
event
An event is used to indicate that an action was taken on a component, usually by a program user. Examples of events are a mouse clicked, a key pressed, a button clicked, or a window resized.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.7 - Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.3 - Event Source in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
event dispatch thread
All Swing window events, such as mouse clicks, keyboard input, component repaint, and more are performed on a separate thread, called the event dispatch thread, also referred to as the EDT.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.1 - Create a Standard Project and Class.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.5 - Create a Thread.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.6 - Stop a Thread.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 3.2 - Pause the Event Dispatch Thread.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.2 - Stop All Activity with a Sleeping Thread.
event-driven programming
Event-driven programming is a style of programming in which the program sets up the desired environment, then just waits for events. The program then responds to the events as they occur, in whatever order they happen.
See the Introduction in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
event queue
Java's event queue is a list used as a control mechanism for handling events from a window's many different inputs. All Swing components use the event queue for handling events. Components created in the main() method require code to add the component to the event queue.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.9 - Event Queue in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
exception
An exception is an event that occurs while running code, disrupting the code's usual execution flow. For example, an exception will occur if s program tries to convert a string with alphabetic characters into an integer, or if a program tries to read from a file that does not exist. The program should include try/catch blocks containing code for handling anticipated exception occurrences.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - Try/Catch Blocks and Exceptions in Do-It-Yourself Java Games in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Create and Throw Custom Exceptions.
exit code
An exit code is an integer used with System's exit() method, indicating whether the program exited as expected.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - Use System Exit Codes.
export
Exporting a program takes the program out of Eclipse and puts it in a separate JAR file. The program can then be run without Eclipse.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.2 - Export a Program in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Export a Program in Appendix D - Using Eclipse.
extend
A class may already exist that provides functionality close to that needed for a new class. Instead of adding more variables and methods to the first class, and instead of repeating all the first class's variables and methods in the new class, define the new class to extend the first class. The original class then serves as the superclass of the new class.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.7 - Extend the DIYWindow Class in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
extract
Extracting files is the process of copying and decompressing files from a ZIP file or JAR file into another folder on the computer.
See Download and Install Eclipse in Appendix C - Setup.
See Download AdvancedDIYJava.zip Detailed Instructions in Appendix C - Setup.
File
The Java File class allows programs to work with the contents of a file and the file's path name.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.2 - Read Image Files, Subimages, Image Icons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.2 - File Choosers in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Lesson 9.2 - Box Layout, Combined Layouts in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.7 - Add Sound.
See Lesson 2.1 - Drag Objects, Use a Dictionary.
file chooser
A file chooser is a dialog that allows the user to browse through a list of files on his computer and choose a file to use in the program. Create a file chooser using JFileChooser.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.2 - File Choosers in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
file filter
A file filter applied to a file chooser will restrict the files in the chooser's list by some criteria. For example, a file filter could be added to include only those files with a specific file name extension. Create a file filter using the FileFilter class.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.3 - An Image File Filter in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
FileFilter
FileFilter is the class that should be extended to create a file filter.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.3 - An Image File Filter in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
FileNotFoundException
A FileNotFoundException is an exception thrown when a program tries to read from a file that does not exist.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.2 - Read from a File, Catch Multiple Exceptions in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
FileReader
A FileReader reads character data from a file.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.2 - Read from a File, Catch Multiple Exceptions in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
FileWriter
A FileWriter writes character data to a file.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.1 - Write to a File in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
final
The value of a variable declared with the final attribute is set and then never again changed by the program.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 14.6 - Static Final Variables in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
float
Float is a basic data type in Java. A float variable can hold a decimal number with as many as 7 decimal places. To specify a float value in a program, type the value with a decimal point, add an “f” to the end of the value, and use no quotation marks.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.6 - Double Data Type in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
FlowLayout
The FlowLayout is a layout best used whenever any number of components should be arranged in a row, and each displayed at its preferred size. However, additional rows will be created in a FlowLayout if not all the components fit within the width of the container.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.3 - Multiple Panels, Preferred Size, Dimension in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
focus
The component in focus will receive keyboard input. Only one component will be in focus at a time. Focus is often referred to as keyboard focus.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.2 - In Focus Mark in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.3 - Button Focus in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
focus listener
Focus listeners are classes that extend the FocusListener class. They wait for FocusEvents.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
focus mark
Focus mark refers to the mark that gets painted on a component when the component is in focus. For example, a button will have a rectangle painted around the button's text when the button is in focus.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.2 - In Focus Mark in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
FocusAdapter
A FocusAdapter is a class that eases FocusListener object creation. Using a FocusAdapter, a programmer writes code only for the FocusListener's methods that will be used, rather than having to write code for all the defined FocusListener methods. A FocusAdapter may be used wherever a FocusListener is required.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
FocusEvent
A FocusEvent is an event caused by a component coming into focus or going out of focus. Add a FocusListener to a component to run code when the FocusEvent occurs.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
FocusListener
A FocusListener waits for a FocusEvent from its assigned component. When a FocusEvent occurs, Java calls the FocusListener's focusGained() or focusLost() method.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
font
A font defines how characters will be drawn to the display. A font defines the type design, style, and size of the characters.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.3 - Font in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.2 - Draw Strings, Font Metrics in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
font metrics
Font metrics are the measurements of how text is rendered in a specific font. A font metrics object can calculate the measurements of text, or of portions of character symbols. Use FontMetrics to create font metrics.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.2 - Draw Strings, Font Metrics in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
FontMetrics
FontMetrics is the class used to create a font metrics object.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.2 - Draw Strings, Font Metrics in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
for loop
A for loop is a block of code that repeats a set number of times. A for loop typically initializes an iteration variable, increments or decrements the iteration variable, and terminates when the iteration variable reaches a particular value.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.1 - For Loops in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
foreground color
The foreground color is the color used for the text or symbols that are drawn onto a component. For example, the circle for a radio button will be drawn using the foreground color.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.4 - Foreground Color in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
glue component
Glue components are often added to a container using BoxLayout to add space between other components. Glue components are invisible and all glue components in a container will stretch in size equally to use up any extra space in that row or column. To add an exact amount of space that won't stretch, use a rigid component instead.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.3 - Space Between Components in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
graphical user interface
A graphical user interface, often abbreviated as GUI, is a visual way for program users to interact with a computer. A GUI consists of a window, plus buttons, menus, and any other visual input methods that allow a user to express what he wants the program to do.
See Lesson 2.1 - Border Layout in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
Graphics
The Graphics class allows a program to draw, scale, or rotate the contents of an image, or to draw on a component.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - A Painted Panel: Color, Rectangles, Lines, Circles, and Preferred Size in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - New Graphics, Scale an Image in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.2 - Draw Strings, Font Metrics in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.4 - XOR Mode in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
GridLayout
The GridLayout is a layout best used whenever components should be arranged in a grid, with each section the same size. If components are not all the same size, they will be stretched so they are displayed the same size.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.2 - Grid Layout in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
GUI
GUI stands for Graphical User Interface.
See Lesson 2.1 - Border Layout in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
horizontal alignment
Use a label's setHorizontalAlignment0 method to horizontally align text in a label. Use a container's setAlignmentX() method to horizontally align a component in its container.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.4 - Align Text in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.2 - Box Layout, Combined Layouts in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
if statement
An if statement is a block of code that runs only if the specified test evaluates to true. An if statement may also have an optional else block that runs only if the test evaluates to false.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.1 - If Statements, Strings that are Equal or Contain Letters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
Image
The Image class represents many different kinds of images. Image provides methods that are common to all images. However, Image is an abstract class. To create an Image, a program must use one of Image's subclasses. A BufferedImage is a subclass of Image.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.2 - Read Image Files, Subimages, Image Icons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - New Graphics, Scale an Image in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.2 - Save an Image in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
image button
An image button is a button that displays an image instead of text. Create an image button using JButton and an ImageIcon.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.1 - Buttons with Images in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
image label
An image label is a label that displays an image instead of text. Create an image label using JLabel and an ImageIcon.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
ImageIcon
An ImageIcon object is typically a small image and is easily loaded into the program using the file name or URL. ImageIcons are often used for images on buttons and in labels. An ImageIcon is not a subclass of Image, so an ImageIcon may not be used where Images are expected, nor may an Image be used where an ImageIcon is expected.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.1 - Buttons with Images in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.2 - Read Image Files, Subimages, Image Icons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.2 - Save an Image in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
ImageIO
ImageIO is a class used for reading and writing image files of various types.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.2 - Read Image Files, Subimages, Image Icons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.2 - Save an Image in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.1 - Transparent Colors, PNG Images in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
implement
Java interfaces are associated with a class by including the key word implements in the class's declaration. When a class implements an interface, it must provide code for all methods declared in the interface.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.5 - Create a Thread.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 3.3 - Define a Thread Inline.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.3 - Create an Interface.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.5 - Reuse Game Logic.
import
Java must have the full, proper name of every class it uses in a program, including the class's package name. Use import statements in a class definition to provide the full name of the classes it uses, so the class may refer to those imported classes by name only, without their package names. Import a class by adding an import statement for that class at the beginning of the class definition. Import statements are not needed for classes defined in the java.lang package.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.2 - Generate Random Numbers in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
index
An index is the position of an item in an ordered collection of items. For example, indexes are used to name the position of a character in a string, or an element in an array. The iteration variable in a for loop is also sometimes referred to as the loop index.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.4 - Index of Characters in a String in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 15.3 - Index of Next Character in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
infinite loop
An infinite loop is a block of code that would repeat forever because an end condition is never met. You may have to use the Eclipse terminate button, or reboot the computer, to end an infinite loop.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.3 - Infinite Loops in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
initialize
To initialize a variable, assign its first value.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.3 - Variables, Strings, and the Escape Character in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
inline
Classes may be defined inline, meaning the class is defined within the code of the definition of another class. If the class that is being defined inline is not assigned to a variable, it is called an anonymous inline definition. A class defined inline is sometimes referred to as an inner class.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 3.3 - Define a Thread Inline.
input field
An input field is a component that allows a program user to enter character data to be used by a program. Create an input field using JTextField or JTextArea.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 3.1 - Text Areas in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
input stream
An input stream reads non-character data from a file. Create an input stream using InputStream.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.7 - Put Data Files in the JAR File in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.7 - Add Sound.
InputStream
The InputStream class is used to create an input stream of non-character data.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.7 - Put Data Files in the JAR File in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.7 - Add Sound.
InputStreamReader
The InputStreamReader class is used to read non-character data from an input stream and convert it into character data.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.7 - Put Data Files in the JAR File in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
instance
A class is a definition of an object. An object, or class instance, is created from a class definition.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 16.1 - Objects, Card in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
instance variable
An instance variable is a variable declared in a class definition instead of in a method. Such a variable may be used by any of the methods defined by that class, without the variable being passed to the methods as an argument. Each object created from the class has its own copy of the instance variable.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 14.3 - Instance Variables in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
int
Int is a basic data type in Java. An int variable can hold an integer value between -2,147,483,648 and 2,147,483,647. To specify an int value in a program, type the value without quotation marks.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Integer Data Type and Addition in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
integer
An integer is a whole number value, either positive or negative. An integer value is typed without quotation marks and without a decimal point. Integer variables are declared in Java as “int”, “byte”, “short”, or “long”.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Integer Data Type and Addition in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.2 - Convert a String to an Integer in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.5 - Integer Subtraction, Multiplication, and Division in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
interface
An interface is a Java construct containing only method declarations and final static variables. All declared methods will be required to be defined in any class that implements the interface. Starting with Java 8, interfaces may also include fully defined static methods and fully defined default methods. Interface default methods are not used in this book.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.5 - Create a Thread.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.3 - Create an Interface.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.4 - Use an Interface for State-Driven Design.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.5 - Reuse Game Logic.
IOException
An IOException is an exception thrown when an error occurs as a program tries to read from or write to a file. For example, the IOException is thrown if a file that exists can't be opened.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.1 - Write to a File in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.2 - Read from a File, Catch Multiple Exceptions in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
iteration variable
An iteration variable is a variable declared in a for loop, incremented or decremented each time through the loop, and compared against another value as a loop exit test. The iteration variable, sometimes also called the loop index or loop control variable, is used to control the number of times a for loop runs.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.1 - For Loops in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
JAR file
A JAR file is a Java Archive file. It contains one or more folders or files of Java code. A JAR file is named with “.jar” as its extension. If a JAR file is created as a Java executable file, the program in the JAR file can be run by simply double-clicking on the name of the JAR file.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.1 - Java Projects and Packages in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.2 - Export a Program in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.7 - Put Data Files in the JAR File in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
Java project
A Java project is the highest level of organization of Java code in Eclipse. Each program in this book is organized as a separate Java project in Eclipse. A Java project contains one or more packages, and each package contains one or more class definitions. Most of the Java projects in this book contain only one package because these programs are relatively small.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.1 - Java Projects and Packages in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Create a First Project in Appendix D - Using Eclipse.
JButton
JButton is the class used to create a button.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.7 - Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.1 - A Custom Button, this in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.1 - Another Custom Button in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.1 - Buttons with Images in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
JDialog
JDialog is the class used to a create custom dialog.
