See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.1 - A Custom Dialog in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
JFileChooser
JFileChooser is the class used to create a file chooser.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.2 - File Choosers in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
JFrame
JFrame is the class used to create a window.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.1 - A Standard Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Add Text, Window Size in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.5 - Pack a Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.6 - Disable Resizing in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.7 - Window Title, Center in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
JLabel
JLabel is the class used to create a label.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Add Text, Window Size in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
JMenu
JMenu is the class used to create a menu.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
JMenuBar
JMenuBar is the class used to create a menu bar.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
JMenuItem
JMenuItem is the class used to create a menu item.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
JOptionPane
JOptionPane is the class that eases displaying a message dialog or a confirm dialog.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.8 - Message Dialogs in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.4 - Confirm Dialogs in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
JPanel
JPanel is the class used to create a panel.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.2 - Panels, Predefined Colors in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
JPEG
JPEG is a format for image files. JPEG stands for Joint Photographic Experts Group. A JPEG file is usually named with “.jpg” as its extension.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.2 - Save an Image in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.1 - Transparent Colors, PNG Images in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
JRadioButton
JRadioButton is the class used to create a radio button.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
JScrollPane
JScrollPane is the class used for adding scroll bars to any component.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 3.2 - Scroll Bars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
JTextArea
JTextArea is the class used to create a large text field that consists of multiple rows and columns. JTextAreas are usually used as input fields.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 3.1 - Text Areas in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
JTextField
JTextField is the class used to create a text input field.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
JToolBar
JToolBar is the class used to create a toolbar.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
key code
A key code of a KeyEvent is a number that represents the keyboard key that was pressed. Key codes are static integer variables whose name starts with VK_. A key code represents which key was pressed, not the character value of that key. VK stands for virtual key.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listener in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
key listener
A key listeners is a class that extends the KeyListener class. A key listener waits for KeyEvents.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
KeyAdapter
A KeyAdapter is a class that eases KeyListener object creation. Using a KeyAdapter, a programmer writes code only for the KeyListener's methods that will be used, rather than having to write code for all the methods defined in KeyListener. A KeyAdapter may be used wherever a KeyListener is required.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
keyboard input
Keyboard input refers to data that comes to a program as a result of a user pressing keys on a keyboard. Input fields could be used to receive keyboard input. Or a key listener could be created to listen for keyboard input.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
KeyEvent
A KeyEvent is an event caused by a program user pressing a key on a keyboard. Add a KeyListener to a component to run code when the KeyEvent occurs.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
KeyListener
A KeyListener waits for a KeyEvent from its assigned component. When a KeyEvent occurs, Java calls the KeyListener's keyPressed(), keyReleased(), or keyTyped() method.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
keystroke
A keystroke is the act of pressing a keyboard key. Programs can process data about a keystroke that includes any modifiers added to the key, such as Alt, Ctrl, Shift, or mouse button down.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
label
A label usually consists of a single line of text displayed in a container. However, an image or a combination of an image and text can also serve as a label. Create a label using JLabel.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Add Text, Window Size in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
layout
A container's layout defines how components will be arranged in the container. Java calculates the best fit, considering each component's size, the layout chosen, and the system's defined look and feel. Layouts explained in the book More Do-It-Yourself Java Games include BorderLayout, BoxLayout, FlowLayout, and GridLayout.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.1 - Border Layout in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.3 - Multiple Panels, Preferred Size, Dimension in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.2 - Grid Layout in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.2 - Box Layout, Combined Layouts in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
library
Eclipse refers to an external JAR file as a library. For example, DIYJava.jar is a JAR file that must be added as a library in the build path of any Java project that uses the DIYWindow class.
See Lesson 1.1 - Java Projects and Packages in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
listen
Code listens for a user action on a component, waiting for a specific kind of event. Each type of user action requires a different type of listener.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.7 - Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.3 - Event Source in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listener in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listener, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
listener
A listener is code written to listen for events. Different kinds of events, such as when a program user clicks a mouse button, may be recognized by a different type of listener, such as a mouse listener. Each type of listener, such as a MouseListener, is defined in a separate class. Each class provides different methods for processing an event, such as mousePressed() or mouseReleased().
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.7 - Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
listing
A program listing usually shows all the code for that program. The listings in this book are only partial listings. They use an ellipsis, …, to indicate where code from the program is not shown.
See Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Appendix B - Completed Listings.
logic
Program logic refers to how program objects interact to enable a program to accomplish its intent. This program logic is also sometimes referred to more specifically to its purpose as game logic, domain logic, or business logic.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - Set up Game Logic in the “Model”.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.5 - Reuse Game Logic.
logical AND operator
The logical AND operator, &&, is used to determine whether two tests both evaluate to true. If the test on the left side is false, Java does not perform the test on the right side.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.1 - If Statements, Strings that are Equal or Contain Letters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
logical OR operator
The logical OR operator, ||, is used to determine whether at least one of two tests evaluates to true. If the test on the left side is true, Java does not perform the test on the right side.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.1 - If Statements, Strings that are Equal or Contain Letters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
long
A long is a basic data type in Java. A long variable can hold an integer value between -9,223,372,036,854,775,808 and 9,223,372,036,854,775,807. To specify a long value in a program, type the value without quotation marks.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Integer Data Type and Addition in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
look and feel
The look and feel of a system refers to how an operating system displays components and how the components work on that operating system (for example Windows, OS X, or Linux). Most often, a Java programmer will set a program to use either the system look and feel or the cross-platform look and feel. Using the system look and feel, a program's display appearance and behavior may vary when run on each operating system. Using the cross-platform look and feel, the program's display appearance and behavior will be the same when run on any operating system, but may not match the display appearance or behavior of other types of programs run on a particular operating system.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.10 - Cross Platform Look and Feel in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
main() method
The main() method is the first method called when a program starts.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
maximized
When a window is maximized, it fills the entire display area of the computer's monitor or screen.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.6 - Window Size and Position in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
menu
A menu is a drop down list of one or more choices, called menu items, on a menu bar. Use JMenu to create a menu.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
menu bar
A menu bar is a row of one or more menus, usually stretched across the top of a container. Use JMenuBar to create a menu bar.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
menu item
A menu item is a clickable choice in a menu. When the menu item is clicked, an ActionEvent is sent. If the program is listening for the event, the program will usually respond in some way. Use JMenuItem to create a menu item.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
message dialog
A message dialog is a dialog whose purpose is simply to display a message.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.8 - Message Dialogs in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
method
A method is a named block of code that can be called from within the program.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.3 - Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - Methods with Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.3 - Methods that Return a Value in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Static Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.3 - Methods with Multiple Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
minimized
When a window is minimized, it is removed from the screen but the program that displayed it is still running and accessible. In Microsoft Windows, a minimized window is displayed as an icon in the task bar. Clicking on the window's icon in the task bar will return the window to the display, at the window's previous location, and having its previous size.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.6 - Window Size and Position in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
modal
A dialog may be modal or non-modal. When a modal dialog is displayed, the program stops to wait for the user to close the dialog. Use a modal dialog if the program should wait for user input before proceeding.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.3 - Get Dialog Data in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
model
In a model/view/controller design approach, the model holds the domain objects and the logic that define how the objects interact in the domain.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - Set up Game Logic in the “Model”.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.5 - Reuse Game Logic.
model/view/controller
Model/View/Controller design organizes code into three separate categories: The model holds the domain objects and logic that define how the objects interact in the domain. The view presents the program's information to the user and allows user input into the program. The controller interprets the domain object data and controls the flow of information between the model and the view.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Lay out the Display in the “View”.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - Set up Game Logic in the “Model”.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.5 - Reuse Game Logic.
modulo
Modulo is the remainder after dividing two numbers.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 16.3 - Modulo in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
mouse listener
A mouse listeners is a class that extends the MouseListener class. A mouse listener waits for MouseEvents.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.1 - Drag Objects, Use a Dictionary.
mouse motion listener
A mouse motion listener is a class that extends the MouseMotionListener class. A mouse listener waits for MouseEvents.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.1 - Drag Objects, Use a Dictionary.
MouseAdapter
A MouseAdapter is a class that eases MouseListener object creation. Using a MouseAdapter, a programmer writes code only for the MouseListener's methods that will be used, rather than having to write code for all the methods defined in MouseListener. A MouseAdapter may be used wherever a MouseListener is required.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.1 - Drag Objects, Use a Dictionary.
MouseEvent
A MouseEvent is an event caused by a program user clicking a mouse button. Add a MouseListener or a MouseMotionListener to a component to run code when a MouseEvent occurs.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.1 - Drag Objects, Use a Dictionary.
MouseListener
A MouseListener waits for a MouseEvent from its assigned component. When a MouseEvent occurs, Java calls the MouseListener's mouseClicked(), mouseEntered(), mouseExited(), mousePressed(), or mouseReleased() method.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
MouseMotionAdapter
A MouseMotionAdapter is a class that eases MouseMotionListener object creation. Using a MouseMotionAdapter, a programmer writes code only for the MouseMotionListener's methods that will be used, rather than having to write code for all the methods defined in MouseMotionListener. A MouseMotionAdapter may be used wherever a MouseMotionListener is required.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
MouseMotionListener
A MouseMotionListener waits for a MouseEvent from its assigned component. When a MouseEvent occurs, Java calls the MouseMotionListener's mouseDragged() or mouseMoved() method.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
non-character data
Character data is data made up of characters that can be inserted into strings. Non-character data is data made up of bit-patterns, such as image file data, that cannot be inserted into strings.
non-modal
A dialog may be modal or non-modal. When a non-modal dialog is displayed, the program continues to run. Use a non-modal dialog if the dialog should remain displayed while the program user continues interacting with the rest of the program.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.3 - Get Dialog Data in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
not operator
The not operator, !, inverts the value of a boolean or returns the complement of a test evaluation. For example, !true returns false.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.1 - If Statements, Strings that are Equal or Contain Letters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
NumberFormatException
A NumberFormatException is an exception thrown if a program cannot successfully convert a value to a number. For example, if a program tries to convert “abc” to a number, that program will throw a NumberFormatException.
See Lesson 8.4 - Try/Catch Blocks and Exceptions in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
object
An object is an instance of a class. The object holds the information defined in the class and can be operated on by the class's methods.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 16.1 - Objects, Card in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
Object
A Java class named Object is the base class of all Java classes.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.3 - Event Source in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
override
Consider overriding a method whenever a superclass provides a method that you want to operate differently in a class you define. To override a method, create a method in your class, with the exact same name, static modifier, return type, and parameters as the method defined(define) in the superclass. The visibility of your method need not be identical to, but cannot be more visible, than the method it overrides.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Create a Standard Custom Panel.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.2 - Integrate the Timer.
pack
Packing a window tells Java to resize the window and arrange all of its components in the smallest possible area, considering all the components' layouts and preferred sizes.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.5 - Pack a Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
package
Packages contain one or more class files that are typically used together.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.1 - Java Projects and Packages in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Create a First Package in Appendix D - Using Eclipse.
panel
A panel is a container that can hold many components, including other panels. Use JPanel to create panels.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.2 - Panels, Predefined Colors in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.3 - Multiple Panels, Preferred Size, Dimension in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
Panels are also often used as drawing surfaces for program-created objects for which Java has no components, such as dice, letter tiles, and cards.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - A Painted Panel: Color, Rectangles, lines, Circles, and Preferred Size in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
parameter
Methods are defined to expect zero or more input values, referred to as arguments. These expected input values are declared in the method as parameters, each with a variable type and name. The method then uses those variables to access the value of the argument passed to the method when the method is called.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - Methods with Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.3 - Methods with Multiple Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
pass
Passing a value to a method with defined parameters means the program sends the value to the method as an argument, when the method is called.
See Lesson 7.1 - Methods with Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
PNG
PNG is a format for image files. “PNG” stands for Portable Network Graphics. A PNG file is usually named with “.png” as its extension.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.1 - Transparent Colors, PNG Images in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
Point
A Point is a class that holds two integers, usually representing x and y coordinates.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.6 - Window Size and Position in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
preferred size
A component's preferred size consists of a programmer's desired width and height values (a Dimension) for the component. Some layouts display components at their preferred size, others do not.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.3 - Multiple Panels, Preferred Size, Dimension in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
Always provide the preferred size of a panel that holds no components, such as a panel used as a drawing surface, by overriding the panel's getPreferredSize() method. Otherwise that panel might have no reserved space in the layout.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - A Painted Panel: Color, Rectangles, Lines, Circles, and Preferred Size in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
primitive
The Java primitive data types are int, double, char, boolean, byte, short, long, and float. The primitive types require no class definitions, and are manipulated using language-defined operations, rather than by calling methods.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 15.5 - Array Lists in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
private
A variable or method declared as private can only be used in the declaring class.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.3 - Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.7 - Extend the DIYWindow Class in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Static Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 14.3 - Instance Variables in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
protected
A protected variable or method is normally only used within its own class or subclass. However, it may also be accessed by an object created from its class's class or subclass as long as the object is created in the same package.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.7 - Extend the DIYWindow Class in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
public
A variable or method declared as public can be accessed by an object created from its class's class or subclass, in any class in the same build path.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.7 - Extend the DIYWindow Class in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Static Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 14.3 - Instance Variables in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
Quick Fix
The Quick Fix feature of Eclipse lists ways Eclipse thinks a syntax error could be fixed. To use Quick Fix, rest your mouse on the underlined error in the code. Eclipse will list ways to fix the problem. Select one of the options and Eclipse will fix the error for you.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
radio button
A radio button is a clickable component with text. A radio button has only two states: selected or not selected. Use JRadioButton to create radio buttons. Radio buttons are usually added to a button group, in which only one radio button may be selected at a time. Use ButtonGroup to create button groups.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
repaint
When a program repaints a component, the program asks Java to draw the entire component again. A component should be repainted whenever the program changes variable values that might affect how the component should look. Use the component's repaint() method to repaint the component. The program should revalidate instead of repaint the component after adding or removing objects displayed on the component.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - A Painted Panel: Color, Rectangles, Lines, Circles, and Preferred Size in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.3 - Reduce Animation Flicker.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.2 - Stop All Activity with a Sleeping Thread.
resolved
Getting a syntax error that a variable name cannot be resolved means the variable is not yet defined. This error may be fixed by declaring the variable either as an instance or static variable or as a local variable in the method before the variable is used.
See Lesson 7.1 - Methods with Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games
Getting a syntax error that a class name cannot be resolved means the class is not yet defined or not accessible. This error is usually fixed by using Quick Fix to import the needed class. If Quick Fix does not list the class, you may need to add the class's library or Java project to the build path for the current Java project.
See Lesson 9.2 - Generate Random Numbers in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
resource
A program's resources include any additional files that are needed to allow the program to run. The resources often include data files and image files.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.7 - Put Data Files in the JAR File in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
return
A method may optionally return a value. One ore more return statements can be coded in a method. Whenever a return statement is run, control flow returns to the code that called the method. If a method returns a value, the code that called the method may assign the results of that call to a variable of the same type as the returned value.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.3 - Methods that Return a Value in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
revalidate
When a program revalidates a component, the program is asking Java to again perform the layout of that component and any contained components. A program should revalidate a component when the program adds, removes, or resizes any component object within that component.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.3 - Add and Remove Components in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - A Painted Panel: Color, Rectangles, Lines, Circles, and Preferred Size in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
rigid component
Rigid components are often added to a BoxLayout to add space between components. Rigid components are invisible, but will take up the exact amount of space defined for them. Use a glue component instead if an invisible component is needed that should stretch to fill remaining space.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.3 - Space Between Components in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
root pane
A JFrame window is actually made up of several panes, one of which is the root pane. Explanation of all these panes is beyond the scope of this book. However, you need to know that to use a button as a default button, a program must get the JFrame object's root pane, and set its default button.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.6 - A Default Button in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
row-major order
Java arrays are stored in row-major order. Row-major order means data is stored for the first dimension first, followed by the second, etc. If an array is defined as having two dimensions, row and column, with row being its first dimension, Java would store all the data for row 1, then the data for row 2, etc.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.1 - Use a Multi-Dimensional Array.
run
When a program is run, Java calls the program's main() method and runs the instructions of each line of code in sequence.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
Runnable
Runnable is an interface whose only method is run().
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.5 - Create a Thread.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 3.3 - Define a Thread Inline.
scroll bars
Scroll bars are slider components that are added to the side and/or bottom of another component 's display if that other component does not fit in its container. Sliders allow a program user to scroll through the parts of the component that did not fit on the display. To easily add scroll bars to a component, put it in a JScrollPane.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 3.2 - Scroll Bars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
serial version UID
The serial version UID is meant to be a unique ID assigned to the current version of a class. The serial version UID is only used if its defining class is serialized. None of the classes in this book will be serialized, and serialization is beyond the scope of this book. You may ignore the warning Eclipse gives about the missing serialVersionUID given when you extend one of the Java Swing classes.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.8 - Serial Version UID in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
short
Short is a basic data type in Java. A short variable can hold an integer value between -32,768 and 32,767. To specify a short value in a program, type the value without quotation marks.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Integer Data Type and Addition in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
SimpleDateFormat
SimpleDateFormat is a class that defines how a Date is to be displayed as a string. For example, a SimpleDateFormat may include month names or month numbers, it may include the time or only the day, and it may include extra characters: comma, slash, dash, colon, or others.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.4 - Current Date, Date Format in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
source
Many events define a method for getting the source of the event. Getting the source will return the component on which the event occurred.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.3 - Event Source in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
stack trace
A stack trace may be used to get more information about an exception that is thrown. A printed stack trace consists of the exception's message, followed by a list of the method calls and the classes from which they were called, that preceded the exception. Use Exception's printStackTrace() method to print a stack trace to the console.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Create and Throw Custom Exceptions.
state-driven programming
State-driven programming is designing code to control program activity based on the defined possible states of an object or program. The program determines which methods to call based on the current state's value. The methods then change the state's value as appropriate. State-driven code may be written using a switch block or if statements, or it may be written using state objects whose classes implement a state interface.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.1 - Use State-Driven Programming, Detect Collisions of Non-Rectangular Shapes.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.4 - Use an Interface for State-Driven Design.
statement
A statement is a complete line of code, usually up to and including the ending semicolon. Some statements, such as if statements and switch statements, include a block of code. Such statements end after the block of code instead of after a semicolon.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.1 - If Statements, Strings that are Equal or Contain Letters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.2 - Switch Statements in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - While Loops in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.1 - For Loops in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
static
Static methods are self-contained. They can only use their parameter values and static variables; they cannot use the class's instance variables. A static method may be called by using its class name followed by the method name.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Static Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
Static variables are shared by every object created from the class. If one object updates the value of a static variable, all objects created from that class see the same new value for that variable. Static variables must be declared in a class definition, not in a method.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 14.6 - Static Final Variables in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
string
A string is text with zero or more characters of any kind. String variables are declared in Java as “String”. To specify a string value in a program, type the text surrounded with double quotation marks.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.3 - Variables, Strings, and the Escape Character in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.2 - Convert a String to an Integer in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.1 - Order of Operation in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.2 - String Length and Substring in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.4 - Index of Characters in a String in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 14.2 - Replace Characters in a String in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
stub
Stub code is an automatically-generated method declaration. The content of the method is left empty for the programmer to write himself.
See Create a First Program in Appendix D - Using Eclipse.
subimage
A subimage is a rectangular portion of an image.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.2 - Read Image Files, Subimages, Image Icons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
super()
Use super() as the first line of code in a method to call that method in the class's superclass.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.2 - Integrate the Timer.
superclass
A superclass is a class from which the current class is derived. All classes without a defined superclass have Object as their superclass. Any class may be used as a superclass. An object created from a class is considered to be “a kind of” its superclass, and may use any of the public or protected variables or methods of its superclass. For example, a class which names DIYWindow as its superclass is a kind of DIYWindow and may use the print() and input() methods defined by DIYWindow.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.7 - Extend the DIYWindow Class in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Create a First Program in Appendix D - Using Eclipse.
Swing
Java Swing is the collection of user interface components in the javax package. Swing component names all start with a J, such as JFrame, JPanel, and JButton.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.1 - Create a Standard Project and Class.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.1 - Animate with a Swing Timer.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.3 - Reduce Animation Flicker.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Lay out the Display in the “View”.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.2 - Stop All Activity with a Sleeping Thread.
switch statement
A switch statement is a block of code that runs different code for each expected value of a variable.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.2 - Switch Statements in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.4 - Switch Default in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.6 - Case without Break in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 15.1 - Switch Statement with Integers in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
syntax error
A syntax error occurs if code does not meet the order or content rules required by Java. All syntax errors must be fixed before a program can run. Eclipse provides a Quick Fix tool to easily fix syntax errors.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
task bar
Microsoft Windows has a task bar, usually displayed across the bottom of the screen, that contains an icon for each program that currently displays a window. Clicking any of the icons in the task bar brings the selected window to the front of the other windows.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.7 - Window Title, Center in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
text field
A text field is a component that allows a program user to enter one line of character data to be used as input to the program. Create a text field using JTextField.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
thread
A thread is a mechanism that allows each line of code assigned to the thread to run one line at a time along its designed code path. Multiple threads allows multiple code paths to run at the same time, one code path per thread. Every program runs in a main thread. Every program that uses Swing functionality runs a main thread and its Swing operations run in an event dispatch thread. Audio is played in yet another thread. There are many ways to create additional threads. This book creates addition threads using the Thread class or the Swing Timer class.
Thread is the Java class used to create a new thread.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.4 - Pause a Thread.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.5 - Create a Thread.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.6 - Stop a Thread.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 3.2 - Pause the Event Dispatch Thread.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 3.3 - Define a Thread Inline.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.1 - Animate with a Swing Timer.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.3 - Reduce Animation Flicker.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.2 - Stop All Activity with a Sleeping Thread.
throw an exception
When a running program encounters an exception, the program skips to the code that catches that particular exception. If no catch block was written for that exception, the program terminates.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - Try/Catch Blocks and Exceptions in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Lesson 7.1 - Use System Exit Codes.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Create and Throw Custom Exceptions.
Timer
Timer is a class in the Swing package whose start() method will repeatedly call its actionPerformed() method at set intervals. You must provide code for the actionPerformed() method when you create a Timer. Timer runs in a separate thread.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.1 - Animate with a Swing Timer.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.3 - Reduce Animation Flicker.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.2 - Stop All Activity with a Sleeping Thread.
title
Set the title of a program using JFrame's setTitle() method.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.7 - Window Title, Center in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
toolbar
A toolbar is a row of components, typically displayed across the top of a window. Components in a toolbar are most often added as image buttons, but may also include any other types of components. A listener should be programmed for each component in a toolbar, to perform an action when an event occurs on that component.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
tool tip
Because toolbar components often display images instead of text, the corresponding tool's purpose might not always be obvious. Help the program user understand the tool's purpose by displaying a tool tip. A tool tip is the text displayed when the user rests his cursor on a tool image in the toolbar.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
try/catch block
A try/catch block consists of a try block and one or more catch blocks. Place code that might throw an exception within a try block. Place code to be run for each expected exception in a catch block at the end of the try block. When an exception is thrown from within a try block, Java breaks out of the try block and runs the code in the corresponding catch block, before continuing with the code that follows the try/catch block. If there is no catch block for the thrown exception, Java breaks out of the current method and throws the exception to the code that called the method. If no calling method catches the exception, the program ends with a run-time error.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - Try/Catch Blocks and Exceptions in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
type
In Java, the type of an object is defined by its class or its superclass. For example, the HelloWorld class created in the first book is a type of DIYWindow; or a variable declared as a String has String as its type.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
unhandled exception
An unhandled exception is an exception for which no handling code is provided. Add a try/catch block to handle exceptions. A program will stop with a run time error if the program runs into an unhandled exception.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - Try/Catch Blocks and Exceptions in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
unicode
Unicode provides a common representation of text characters that is meant to be independent of the device, program, or language that is working with the text. Unicode numbers have been assigned for all of the typable characters as well as for many symbols not found on a keyboard, such as hearts, diamonds, clubs, and spades.
See Lesson 13.1 - Transparent Colors, PNG Images in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
unzip
Unzip is the process of extracting files from a ZIP file.
See Download and Install Eclipse in Appendix C - Setup.
user
The user is the person who is running a program.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.1 - Input a String in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
variable
A variable is a named piece of data whose value can be changed.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.3 - Variables, Strings, and the Escape Character in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 3.1 - Reuse Strings in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
view
In a model/view/controller design approach, the view is the user interface. The view displays what happens in the model and handles user interactions with the program.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Lay out the Display in the “View”.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.3 - Define Listeners in a Different Class.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - Set up Game Logic in the “Model”.
visible
If a variable or method is visible, it can be accessed by other code. The three different visibility settings are private, protected, and public.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.3 - Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.7 - Extend the DIYWindow Class in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Static Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 14.3 - Instance Variables in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
A window or dialog must be made visible for it to be displayed. To make a window or dialog visible or invisible, use JFrame's or JDialog's setVisible() method. Instead of closing a dialog after the user enters input, make the dialog not visible so the program can still access the data that the user entered.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.1 - A Standard Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.1 - A Custom Dialog in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.3 - Get Dialog Data in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
while loop
A while loop is a block of code that repeats while an expression evaluates to true.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - While Loops in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
window
A basic window consists of a large rectangular viewing area on a screen, usually having a title bar displayed across the top, and a border displayed around its edges. Many other components can be added to a window. Use Java's JFrame class to create a window.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.1 - A Standard Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
window listener
A window listener is a class that extends the WindowListener class. A window listener waits for WindowEvents.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.6 - Window Size and Position in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
window state listener
A window state listener is a class that extends the WindowStateListener class. A window state listener waits for WindowEvents.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
WindowAdapter
WindowAdapter is a class that eases WindowListener object creation. Using a WindowAdapter, a programmer must write code only for the WindowListener's methods that will be used, rather than having to write code for all the methods defined in WindowListener. A WindowAdapter may be used wherever a WindowListener is required.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.6 - Window Size and Position in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
WindowEvent
A WindowEvent is an event caused by a window being: opened, closed, newly made active, made no longer active, minimized, or returned to normal size. Add a WindowListener or a WindowStateListener to a component to run code when the WindowEvent occurs.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.6 - Window Size and Position in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
WindowListener
A WindowListener waits for a WindowEvent from its assigned component. When a WindowEvent occurs, Java calls the WindowListener's windowActivated(), windowClosed(), windowClosing(), windowDeactivated(), windowDeiconified(), windowIconified(), or windowOpened() method.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.6 - Window Size and Position in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
WindowStateListener
A WindowStateListener waits for a WindowEvent from its assigned component. When a WindowEvent occurs, Java calls the WindowStateListener's windowStateChanged() method.
See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
work folder
Create a work folder to contain all the Java code and other files needed for your programs.
See Create a Java Work Folder in Appendix C - Setup.
wrapper
A wrapper exists for each of the Java primitives and may be used to convert a Java primitive value into an object. For example, Integer is a wrapper for integers. You can create an Integer object called obj from an int called num by using Integer obj = new Integer(num).
See Key Points and More in Lesson 15.6 - Array Lists in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
ZIP file
A ZIP file contains the compressed contents of one or more folders or files. A ZIP file is named with “.zip” as its extension. Files must be extracted from a ZIP file before they can be used.
See Download and Install Eclipse in Setup in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.
See Download and Install Eclipse in Appendix C - Setup.

        line = in.readLine();
      }

    }

  private void clicked(int x, int y) {
    int row = y / Cell.SIZE;
    int col = x / Cell.SIZE;
    
    int direction = getSwapDirection(x, y);
    
    switch(direction) {
    case DIRECTION_LEFT :
      swap(row, col, row, col - 1);
      break;
    case DIRECTION_RIGHT :
      swap(row, col, row, col + 1);
      break;
    case DIRECTION_UP :
      swap(row, col, row - 1, col);
      break;
    case DIRECTION_DOWN :
      swap(row, col, row + 1, col);
      break;  
    }
  }

  private int markChainsAndGetPointsInCol(int col) {
    int points = 0;
    
    // get the color of the first ball
    int color = cells[0][col].getColor();
    int count = 1;
 
    // loop through each row of the column
    for (int row = 1; row < ROWS; row++) {
 
      // count the balls in each color
      int nextColor = cells[row][col].getColor();
      if (nextColor == color) {
        count++;
      }
      else {
        color = nextColor;
        count = 1;
      }
      
      // mark chains of three or more. When count  
      // reaches 3, also mark previous two.
      if (count == 3) {
        cells[row][col].setInChain(true);
        cells[row - 1][col].setInChain(true);
        cells[row - 2][col].setInChain(true);
      }
      else if (count > 3) {
        cells[row][col].setInChain(true);
      }
    }
    
    return points;
  }

          movesRemaining = isValidSwap(row, col, DIRECTION_DOWN);
        }
        if (!movesRemaining && col < COLS - 1) {
          movesRemaining = isValidSwap(row, col, DIRECTION_RIGHT);
          
        }
      }
    }
    return movesRemaining;
  }

  private void insertBrick() {
    int brickRow = brick.getRow();
    int brickCol = brick.getColumn();
    int brickRows = brick.getNumberOfRows();
    int brickCols = brick.getNumberOfColumns();
    
    for (int r = 0; r < brickRows; r++) {
      for (int c = 0; c < brickCols; c++) {
        if (brick.hasTileAt(r, c)) {
          int row = r + brickRow;
          int col = c + brickCol;
          board[row][col] = brick.getTileImage();
        }
      }
    }
 
    pickABrick();
  }

    }

      for (int col = 0; col < COLS && filled; col++) {

      if (filled) {

            board[r][c] = board[r - 1][c];
          }
        }
        row++;
        count++;
      }
    }
    
    calculateScore(count);

      }
      in.close();

      line = mazeData.get(0);
      columns = line.length();

  public void draw(Graphics g) {
    for (int row = 0; row < rows; row++) {
      for (int col = 0; col < columns; col++) {
        if (cell[row][col] != TYPE_WALL) {
          int x = col * CELL_SIZE;
          int y = row * CELL_SIZE;
          g.setColor(Color.WHITE);
          g.fillRect(x, y, CELL_SIZE, CELL_SIZE);
          if (cell[row][col] == TYPE_CHEESE) {
            g.setColor(Color.YELLOW);
            g.fillOval(x + QUARTER_CELL_SIZE, y + QUARTER_CELL_SIZE, HALF_CELL_SIZE, HALF_CELL_SIZE);
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }

  }

  private void initGUI() {
    setFocusable(true);
    requestFocusInWindow();
    
    // listeners
    addKeyListener(new KeyAdapter() {
      public void keyPressed(KeyEvent e) {
        int direction = Mouse.DIRECTION_NONE;
        int code = e.getKeyCode();
        switch(code) {
        case KeyEvent.VK_UP :
          direction = Mouse.DIRECTION_UP;
          break;
        case KeyEvent.VK_DOWN :
          direction = Mouse.DIRECTION_DOWN;
          break;
        case KeyEvent.VK_LEFT :
          direction = Mouse.DIRECTION_LEFT;
          break;
        case KeyEvent.VK_RIGHT :
          direction = Mouse.DIRECTION_RIGHT;
          break;
        }
        if (direction != Mouse.DIRECTION_NONE) {
          mouse.turn(direction);
          repaint();
        }
      }
    });
      ...

  public void turn(int direction) {
    this.direction = direction;
    switch(direction) {
    case DIRECTION_UP :
      changeX = 0;
      changeY = -1;
      break;
    case DIRECTION_DOWN :
      changeX = 0;
      changeY = 1;
      break;
    case DIRECTION_LEFT :
      changeX = -1;
      changeY = 0;
      break;
    case DIRECTION_RIGHT :
      changeX = 1;
      changeY = 0;
      break;
    }
  }

  private boolean wallInDirection(int direction) {
    boolean wall = false;
    int checkX = x;
    int checkY = y;
    
    switch(direction) {
    case DIRECTION_UP :
      checkY = y - speed;
      break;
    case DIRECTION_DOWN :
      int imageHeight = image[direction].getHeight();
      checkY = y + speed + imageHeight + 1;
      break;
    case DIRECTION_LEFT :
      checkX = x - speed;
      break;
    case DIRECTION_RIGHT :
      int imageWidth = image[direction].getWidth();
      checkX = x + speed + imageWidth + 1;
      break;
    }
    
    if (maze.wallAt(checkX, checkY)) {
      wall = true;
    }
    
    return wall;
  }

  public void moveIntoCell() {
    int intoX = x % Maze.CELL_SIZE;
    int intoY = y % Maze.CELL_SIZE;
    
    switch(direction) {
    case DIRECTION_UP :
      if (intoY > offsetY[direction]) {
        // center in this cell
        y -= intoY;
      }
      break;
    case DIRECTION_DOWN :
      if (intoY > offsetY[direction]) {
        // center in next cell
        y = y - intoY + Maze.CELL_SIZE;
      }
      break;
    case DIRECTION_LEFT :
      if (intoX > offsetX[direction]) {
        // center in this cell
        x -= intoX;
      }
      break;
    case DIRECTION_RIGHT :
      if (intoX > offsetX[direction]) {
        // center in next cell
        x = x - intoX + Maze.CELL_SIZE;
      }
      break;
    }
  }

  private void readCardImages() {
    BufferedImage cardsImage = FileIO.readImageFile(this, CARDS_FILE);
    int i = 0;
    for (int suit = 0; suit < SUITS; suit++) {
      for (int rank = 0; rank < RANKS; rank++) {
        int x = rank * CARD_WIDTH;
        int y = suit * CARD_HEIGHT;
        cardImages[i] = cardsImage.getSubimage(x, y, CARD_WIDTH, CARD_HEIGHT);
        i++;
      }
    }
    cardImages[CARD_BACK_INDEX] = FileIO.readImageFile(this, CARD_BACK_FILE);
  }

  public void reset() {
    cards.clear();
    int numberOfSuits = Card.SUITS.length();
    int numberOfRanks = Card.RANKS.length;
    int numberOfCards = numberOfSuits * numberOfRanks;
    for (int id = 0; id < numberOfCards; id++) {
      int cardsSize = cards.size();
      int insertAt = 0;
      if (cardsSize > 0) {
        insertAt = rand.nextInt(cardsSize + 1);
      }
      Card card = new Card(id);
      cards.add(insertAt, card);
    }
  }

  public int addCard(Card newCard) {
    int i = 0;
    int numberOfCards = cards.size();
    boolean done = false;
    while (i < numberOfCards && !done) {
      Card card = cards.get(i);
      if (newCard.isGreaterThan(card)) {
        i++;
      }
      else {
        done = true;
      }
    }
    cards.add(i, newCard);
    return i;
  }

  private void deal() {
    // deal 3 cards to each player
    for (int c = 0; c < 3; c++) {
      for (int p = 0; p < numberOfPlayers; p++) {
        int dealTo = (dealerId + p + 1) % numberOfPlayers;
        if (!players[dealTo].isOut()) {
          Card card = deck.deal();
          players[dealTo].addCard(card);
          controller.showDrawCard(players[dealTo], card);
        }
      }
    }
    state = STATE_NEXT_PLAYER;
    play();

  public int getLowestCardIndex() {
    // get the points in each suit
    int[] pointsInSuits = getPointsInSuits();
    
    // get the suit with the least points
    int worstSuit = 0;
    // worst points should start with a number
    // higher than the maximum possible value.  
    // A hand may hold up to 4 cards, so worst  
    // points must be less than 42.
    int worstPoints = 42;
    for (int i = 0; i < pointsInSuits.length; i++) {
      if (pointsInSuits[i] > 0
          && pointsInSuits[i] < worstPoints) {
        worstPoints = pointsInSuits[i];
        worstSuit = i;
      }
    }
  }

  private void settleBlitz() {
    for (int i = 0; i < numberOfPlayers; i++) {
      if (i != active) {
        if (players[i].hasRapped()) {
          players[i].loseTokens(2);
          controller.showLoseTokens(players[i], 2);
        }
        else if (!players[i].isOut()) {
          players[i].loseTokens(1);
          controller.showLoseTokens(players[i], 1);
        }
      }
    }
    dealerId = getNextDealerId();
    Player dealer = players[dealerId];
    controller.showDealer(dealer);
    state = STATE_END_OF_HAND;
    play();
  }

      if (players[i].isOut()) {

  private void deal() {
    boolean blitz = false;
    
    // deal 3 cards to each player
    for (int c = 0; c < 3; c++) {
      for (int p = 0; p < numberOfPlayers && !blitz; p++) {
        int dealTo = (dealerId + p + 1) % numberOfPlayers;
        if (!players[dealTo].isOut()) {
          Card card = deck.deal();
          players[dealTo].addCard(card);
          controller.showDrawCard(players[dealTo], card);
 
          if (c == 2) {
            int pointsInHand = players[dealTo].getPointsInHand();
            if (pointsInHand == 31) {
              blitz = true;
              active = dealTo;
              controller.showBlitz(players[dealTo]);
              state = STATE_SETTLE_BLITZ;
            }
          }
        }
      }
    }
    
    if (!blitz) {
      // deal a discard
      Card card = deck.deal();
      discardStack.add(card);
      controller.showDealDiscard(card);  
      state = STATE_NEXT_PLAYER;
    }
    play();
  }

Appendix C - Setup
These installation and setup instructions are designed for Microsoft Windows. The programs that you'll download, install, and create could run on any computer that runs with a Windows, OS X, or Linux operating system. However, this book doesn't describe how to install or set up the programming environment for those other systems.
Create a Java Work Folder
You must create your own Java work folder on your computer. I recommend that you put your Java work folder in your Windows user folder, but you can put your work folder anywhere on your computer. I called mine java and put it in my user folder, c:\Users\Annette. Therefore, my Java work folder is c:\Users\Annette\java.
To create a folder in Windows 7, first click Start / Computer to open Windows Explorer. To create a folder in Windows 10, first click Start / File Explorer. Then click on the name of the folder in which you want to create the new folder, and click the New folder button. Enter a name for your new folder.
If you share your computer with someone else who also wants to program in Java, create a different Java work folder for each of you. Your Java work folders must either have different names, or be in different folders.
  1. Create a Java work folder on your computer now.
Download and Install Java
You'll be writing your computer programs in the Java programming language. Your computer needs the free Java Development Kit to generate programs from Java code.
The Java Development Kit only needs to be installed one time on your computer, no matter how many people plan to write Java programs on your computer.
To install the Java Development Kit:
  1. Go to http://www.oracle.com/technetwork/java/javase/downloads/index.html.
  2. Click the download button, pictured below, to download the latest version of the Java Development Kit (JDK) for Java Standard Edition (SE)
  1. Accept the license agreement, as shown in the image below. Download either the Windows x86 or Windows x64 version of the Java Development Kit, depending on which version of Windows you have. Windows x86 is for 32-bit Windows; Windows x64 is for 64-bit Windows.
    1. How do you check whether you have 32-bit or 64-bit Windows? In Windows 7, click Start / Control Panel and double-click on System. In Windows 10, click Start / Settings / System / About. The System Type states whether you have the 32-bit or 64-bit operating system. If your Control Panel doesn't have a System icon, you might have to click the View by drop down list in the top right corner of the Control Panel and choose Small Icons.
  2. Double-click the downloaded .exe file name to install Java. You should be able to take all the installation defaults.
Download and Install Eclipse
Eclipse is a free Java development environment. Eclipse makes typing code easier, identifies programming errors, and even suggests ways to fix those errors.
I recommend that you install Eclipse in your Windows user folder, but you can put Eclipse anywhere on your computer. I put mine in my user folder, c:\Users\Annette.
  1. Go to http://www.eclipse.org/downloads/. Click the download packages link below the download button so you can choose which version of Eclipse to download.
  2. Download either the 32-bit or 64-bit version, of Eclipse IDE for Java Developers, depending on which version of Windows you have, to any location on your computer.
  3. To unzip the downloaded .zip file, right-click on its name, choose Extract all..., and browse to the folder into which you want to install Eclipse. I extracted mine into my user folder, c:/Users/Annette.
    1. If you share your computer with someone else who also wants to write Java programs, extract each person's copy of Eclipse into a different folder.
Create a shortcut on your desktop for Eclipse. These instructions are for Windows 7 and 10:
  1. Open the eclipse folder that was created when you extracted the files from the downloaded .zip file. My eclipse folder is in c:/Users/Annette.
  2. Right-click on eclipse.exe and choose copy.
  3. Right-click on your desktop and choose Paste shortcut.
  4. If you aren't the only one who will use Eclipse for programming on your computer, right-click on the shortcut you just created and rename the shortcut for your use. For example, I might rename mine to Eclipse for Annette.
  5. Repeat steps 1-4 for each person who will use Eclipse on your computer, copying the eclipse.exe file that was extracted for them.
Download AdvancedDIYJava.zip Detailed Instructions
The lessons require a few additional data files. Those files are included in a free .zip file on the Godtland Software website:
  1. Download AdvancedDIYJava.zip from http://www.godtlandsoftware.com/DIYJava/.
  2. To unzip AdvancedDIYJava.zip, right-click on AdvancedDIYJava.zip and choose Extract all.... Use the Browse button to extract the files into your Java work folder. I extracted mine into c:/Users/Annette/java.

Appendix D - Using Eclipse
Set up Eclipse.
  1. Double-click your Eclipse shortcut. This window should appear:
  1. Click the Browse... button to find your Java work folder, as shown in the above screenshot, and then click OK. This window should appear:
  1. Click Workbench to open the main Eclipse window.
Use the Java perspective:
  1. Click Window / Perspective / Open Perspective / Java Browsing. If Java is not in the list, you are probably already in the Java Perspective. Your window Eclipse should look similar to this:
Make more room for writing code:
  1. Close the Task list, and Connect MyLyn as shown in this image:
  1. Move the Outline tab to the bottom of the Package Explorer pane, as shown in this image:
You now have everything you need to create your first program!
Create a First Project
Create your first Java project, called Hello World:
  1. If Eclipse is no longer open:
    1. Double-click the Eclipse shortcut you created on your desktop.
    2. Click OK to use your Java work folder as your workspace.
  2. Right-click in the Package Explorer pane and choose New / Java Project.
  3. Name the Java project Hello World, and select Use Default JRE if it is 1.8 or higher, then click Next as shown below. If the default JRE is less than 1.8, select the option to Use an execution environment JRE of 1.8 or higher.
  1. Click Finish.
The Package Explorer pane should now list the project, Hello World.
Key Points and More
  • Each program in this book will be created in a separate Java project.
  • Code that will be shared between different programs will be created in a separate Java project as well.
  • Right-click in the Package Explorer pane to create a Java project.
  • Eclipse will create a folder on your computer in your Java work folder, named the same as the Java project. Give your Java project a name you want to use for the folder on your computer.
    • You now have a folder called Hello World in your Java work folder.
    • For example, capitalize the first letter of each word and put a space between each word like the Hello World project.
  • The minimum JRE requirement for the programs in this book is Java SE 1.8. When you create the Java Projects in this book, make sure you select an option to use a JRE of 1.8 or higher. Once you select this option for creating a project, Eclipse will default to that option for all Java Projects you create in the future.
Create a First Package
Create a package for your Hello World program in the Hello World project:
  1. Right-click on the Hello World project in the Package Explorer pane and choose New / Package.
  2. Name the package ____________.____________.helloworld, as shown in the image below. Use your own name as part of the package name. I used annette.godtland.helloworld for my package name.
  1. Click Finish.
The Package Explorer pane now shows the package you created in your Hello World project.
Key Points and More
  • Organize your program files into packages in Java projects.
  • Right-click on your project in the Package Explorer pane to create a Java package.
  • Put program files that are usually used together into one package.
    • Because your programs will be small, most of your programs will consist of only one package.
  • Package name rules:
    • Make your package name different from anyone else's package names. Java programmers traditionally use their name, business name, domain name, or e-mail address as the first part of their package names.
    • Use all lowercase letters with no spaces.
    • Use periods between different categories in the package name. For example, if the package name identifies who created the package and what the package will be used for, put a period between the creator and the package's purpose.
  • Java projects are used to organize programs within Eclipse; packages are used to organize programs within Java. Because you're using Eclipse, you'll use both Java projects and packages. If you were to create Java programs without Eclipse, you would probably use only packages.
Create A First Program
Create your first program using the JFrame class as its superclass:
  1. Right-click on your package in the Package Explorer pane and choose New / Class.
  2. Enter HelloWorld for the class name, as shown in the image below. (Hint: there's no space between “Hello” and “World”.)
  3. Click Browse for Superclass.
    1. Enter “jfr” for the type, select JFrame, and click OK.
  4. For Which method stubs(stub) would you like to create?, select only public static void main (String[] args).
  1. Click Finish to create the class.
Eclipse will create code for a HelloWorld class that looks like the following listing.
Listing 0-0, from HelloWorld.java
package annette.godtland.helloworld;
 
import javax.swing.JFrame;
 
public class HelloWorld extends JFrame {
 
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    // TODO Auto-generated method stub
 
  }
 
}
  1. Replace the code in the main() method as indicated in this listing:
Listing 0-1, from HelloWorld.java
package annette.godtland.helloworld;
 
import javax.swing.JFrame;
 
public class HelloWorld extends JFrame {
 
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    HelloWorld hello = new HelloWorld();
    hello.setVisible(true);
  }
 
}
  1. Press Ctrl-S to save the program.
  2. Click the Run button, as shown in this image, to run the program:
A tiny window should appear with nothing in it, like this:
The lessons in this book will put contents into the window.
Key Points and More
  • To create classes, right-click on your package name in the Package Explorer pane.
    • Class names may contain numbers, letters, dollar signs, and underscores. Dollar signs and underscores are usually not used.
    • Blanks or periods aren't allowed in class names.
    • Class names cannot start with a number.
    • Class names typically start with an uppercase letter.
    • If the class name includes more than one word, the first letter of each word is usually uppercase, and the rest of the letters are lowercase.
  • Remove the automatically-generated comments Eclipse creates when you create a class.
  • Press Ctrl-S to save your program.
  • Click the Run button to run your program. The Run button looks like a typical play button.
  • Unless you have syntax errors or are told not to, save and run your program after you make the changes from each code listing. If you have a syntax error, use Quick Fix to fix the error:
    • Rest your mouse on the underlined error in the code. Eclipse will list ways to fix the problem. Select one of the options and Eclipse will fix the error for you.
  • Throughout the lessons, you'll often receive the syntax error that says something couldn't be resolved to a type. If you receive that error, use Quick Fix to import the needed class. The class, along with its package name, will be added to the import statements at the beginning of the file.
  • The JDK has many classes with the same name in more than one package. When you are presented with multiple choices for importing a package and not instructed otherwise, import classes from the java.awt, java.io, and javax.swing packages.
  • Code listings may be more difficult to read if lines of text are word wrapped. To reduce word wrapping, set your e-reader to a smaller font.
  • Click the Completed Listing link below any listing to see how to complete the code. However, you may complete the listing differently, if your code does the same thing or if you like what your code does better.
  • The same options won't be used for every class you create. Be sure to follow the instructions exactly as written when you create each class.
Add a Project to the Build Path
The build path holds the location of the projects and libraries needed for creating the program in the Java project. When a program needs to use code that is in a different project or library, the other project or library must be added to the build path of the program's project.
For example, code that will be shared between multiple programs in this book will be in a separate Java project. The shared project needs to be added to the build path of the project of each program that will use the shared code.
To add additional projects of shared code to a new project as the new project is being created:
  1. Click the Next button.
  2. Click the Projects tab, as shown in the image below.
  3. Click Add....
  4. Select the project to add, then click OK.
  5. Click Finish to finish creating the new project.
To add additional projects of shared code to an existing project:
  1. In the Package Explorer pane, right-click on the existing project and select Build Path / Configure Build Path...
  2. Click the Projects tab, as shown in the image above.
  3. Click Add....
  4. Select the project to add, then click OK.
  5. Click OK to close the Java Build Path window.
Export a Program
You must export a finished program if you want to run it without Eclipse or if you want to run it on a different computer.
If you export your program, it will be made into a JAR file (a Java ARchive file) on your computer. JAR files have names that end with “.jar”. To run the program, double-click on the JAR file name.
To export a program:
  1. Right-click on the Java project name in the Package Explorer pane and choose Export.
  2. Select Java / Runnable JAR File, as shown in the image below, and click Next.
  3. Select the launch configuration for your project. Eclipse creates a launch configuration for every new program you run in Eclipse, and adds the launch configuration to this list. The image below shows selecting the launch configuration for the ASCII Art project which was a program created in the first Do-It-Yourself Java Games book.
  4. Enter a name for the JAR file as the Export destination. Naming the JAR file after the Java project will help you remember what program the JAR file contains. The image below shows the JAR file being named ASCIIArt.jar.
  5. Select the option to Package required libraries into generated JAR, as shown in this image:
  1. Click Finish to complete the export.
To run your program without Eclipse:
  1. Find your newly created JAR file in your Java work folder.
  2. Double-click the JAR file name.
You may copy the JAR file to any other folder or any other computer. However, remember to copy any files in the Java work folder that are used by the program, to the same folder as the JAR file.
Key Points and More
  • Export the program as a JAR file if you want to run the program outside of Eclipse or on a different computer.
  • You can save different versions of your program in different JAR files. Use all the same export options but name a different Export destination for each version of the program.
  • Your exported JAR file for the programs created in this book can be run on any computer running a Windows, OS X, or Linux operating system, if a Java Runtime Environment, version 1.8 or later, is installed.
    • The Java Runtime Environment is already installed on most computers, for running other programs.
    • The Java Runtime Environment was included in the Java Development Kit you installed. Therefore, the Java Runtime Environment also was already installed on your computer.
    • Anyone can download and install just the Java Runtime Environment, without the Java Development Kit, from http://java.com/en/download/index.jsp.
  • If there were any files in the Java work folder that were used by the program, always keep a copy of those files in the same folder as the exported JAR file.
  • The JAR file will contain all the .class files that are in the bin folder of the Java work folder. If you want any other files that are in the bin folder inserted into the JAR file, copy them to the src folder before you export the project.
You should now be ready to try the lessons in this book.

Appendix E - Conventions Used and Other Tips
Throughout this book, actions you are to take are given in a numbered list.
Read the Key Points and More at the end of every lesson to review the lesson and to learn a little more. You don't need to memorize them; you can easily refer to them later, if needed. You'll also learn a lot by doing.
Throughout this book, every code listing is shown in a monospaced font between underscored lines.
Code listings may be more difficult to read if text is word wrapped. To reduce word wrapping, set your e-reader to a smaller font.
Above each listing is the file name for the listed code.
Remove from your program any section of code that is shown in the listing as “(Code was removed from here.)”. Also, remove the automatically-generated comments in every class you create. You'll add your own comments in later lessons.
Changes for you to make to your code are shown in bold in the listings.
Most listings only show a portion of the code from the program file. Each section of code that isn't included in the listing is shown as “...”.
Code that you are to complete yourself is shown in the listings as fill-in blanks, ____________________. Fill in the blanks with zero or more words or symbols.
When not specified as right click, click means to click on the object using the left mouse button.
Click the Completed listing link below any listing if you want to see how to complete the code. However, you'll learn more if you try to complete the code yourself before you look up the answer. You may complete the listing differently, if your code does the same thing or if you like what your code does better.
Remove the automatically-generated comments Eclipse creates when you create a class.
Unless you have syntax errors or are told not to, save and run your program after you make the changes from each code listing. If you have a syntax error, use Quick Fix to fix the error:
Rest your mouse on the underlined error in the code. Eclipse will list ways to fix the problem. Select one of the options and Eclipse will fix the error for you.
Throughout the lessons, you'll often receive the syntax error that says something couldn't be resolved to a type. If you receive that error, use Quick Fix to import the needed class. The class, along with its package name, will be added to the import statements at the beginning of the file.
The JDK has many classes with the same name in more than one package. When you are presented with multiple choices for importing a package and not instructed otherwise, import classes from the java.awt, java.io, and javax.swing packages.
The same options won't be used for every class you create. Be sure to follow the instructions exactly as written when you create each class.
Use the Appendix A - Glossary as a glossary and an index. The glossary has definitions of programming terms as well as links for where to find more information about the term in the Do-It-Yourself Java Games books.
Bookmark Appendix A - Glossary with your e-reader to more easily get to the glossary.
